extracted.intended_audience: writers, orators, and students of rhetoric/classical literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for producing elegant, humorous, plain, or affected prose/verse in the classical (Greek/Attic) rhetorical tradition, with advice on diction, rhythm, imagery, and suitability to medium (stage vs. reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Charm by allusion/reference to other writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Charm may spring from a reference to the verses of another writer (e.g., travesty of Homer increases the charm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusion or deliberate travesty of a well-known passage can increase the charm of a passage; examples include Aristophanes mocking Homer. Use such references when they add a layer of meaning or ironic distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of veiled meanings and colloquial reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain veiled meanings have a touch of common talk about them (e.g., veiled reproaches or ambiguous phrases that sound like ordinary conversation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veiled or colloquial turns can charm and be witty; they should feel like common talk and may include playful ambiguity or double entendre. Example: indirect reproaches at a banquet rendered gracefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantry by contrary-to-expectation (unexpected addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sort of wit in the unexpected — a pleasantry added unexpectedly and often unconnected with preceding matter (example: Cyclops ‘Last of all will I eat—Noman’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such pleasantries derive charm from surprise and lack of logical connexion (called 'griphus'). Use sparingly where surprise is desirable; they work best when the unexpected item is brief and self-contained. Anti-pattern: overuse produces incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Griphus (want of sequence) as a device
rubrics_metrics.description: A want of sequence where the pleasantry has no connexion with what precedes it is called 'griphus'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Griphus can be effective comic ornament—examples include incoherent or digressive speeches used for comic effect (Boulias). Use when deliberate incoherence suits the comic or satyric effect; avoid when clarity or argumentative coherence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and parallelism in sentence members
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity in the members of a sentence often produces a witty effect (e.g., ending both members with the same word to create charm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel or mirrored structures (antithesis/parallelism) can generate wit or charm; the effect may vanish if a crucial repeated word is removed. Use judicious repetition for emphasis or surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proverbs to add sprightliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the graces which relate to subject-matter are those which spring from the use of proverbs; 'in its very nature a proverb is a sprightly thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proverbs add sparkle and authority; composers may use two or three in succession to load style with elegance (Sophron). Beware of overloading or using proverbs that are obscure to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and adaptation of fables
rubrics_metrics.description: A fable, when neatly introduced or suitably adapted to the matter in hand, is very piquant and can be used as a familiar or adapted anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fables (long-established or adapted) can enliven prose; add a personal touch or witty twist to make them sparkle. Avoid forced or irrelevant fables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantry from comic mistakes/revulsion from fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasantry is often the result of a revulsion from fear (e.g., mistaking a strap for a snake), and such comic mistakes are amusing in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ comic misperception or benign fear as a source of humor. Keep the scenario credible enough to provoke sympathy rather than confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons and hyperbole for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons and especially hyperboles (impossible character) produce comic pleasantries (e.g., exaggerations of voracity or size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbole is central to comedy; push to the impossible for laughable effect but avoid hyperbole that strains audience credulity or becomes grotesque rather than funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish laughable (humour) from graceful (charm) styles
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable and the graceful must not be confused: materials, expression, purpose, and results differ—grace uses beautiful subjects and words, humour uses ordinary/common words and low subjects (e.g., Thersites vs. God of Love).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match material and diction to the aim: use elevated, beautiful diction and ornaments for charm; use plain, common words for humour. Confusing the two spoils both (elegance ruins humour; vulgarity degrades grace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbal adornment in humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is spoiled by verbal adornment and is turned into a freak; graces of style good in moderation, whereas the elaboration of humour is like beautifying an ape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep humour linguistically plain; excessive poetic or ornate diction undermines comedic effect. Use ordinary vocabulary and colloquial phrasing for jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'beautiful words' (euphony and noble associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful words appeal pleasantly to the ear or eye, or have noble associations (Theophrastus); euphony (smooth, well-proportioned words) produces elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words for sound (smoothness, proportion, weight) and associative nobility. Examples: prefer forms that avoid hiatus, use vowels for smoothness, and consider doubling of consonants for pleasing clang. But rough words can be used purposefully to imitate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euphony: smooth, rough, well-proportioned, weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Musicians speak of words as 'smooth', 'rough', 'well-proportioned', 'weighty'—smooth words consist mainly of vowels; rough words may imitate force; weight arises from breadth, length, formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for smooth or well-proportioned words for elegance; use roughness selectively for onomatopoeia or force. Consider dialectal forms and phonetic shape when choosing words for euphony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pleasant-sounding names and phonetic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasing in sound are names in which letters create a pleasing clang (double l, double n); Attic writers append 'n' for euphony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible choose names and word forms that have pleasing phonetic patterns; minor orthographic/dialectal choices (e.g., adding an 'n') may improve euphony. Be mindful of dialectal appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance via composition and metric framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Charm and grace may be attained if we frame the composition by measures—in whole measures or half-measures; a general metrical character produces an effect felt even when disguised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce subtle rhythm or cadences into prose (not so obvious as to distract). The metrical character should not force itself on attention but reveal itself on analysis. Use cadence to suit tone: long cadence for elevated/pleasant, brisk for plain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and cadence to imitate content (musical imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of words, long unbroken clauses, and cadence can imitate musical or natural sounds (e.g., long clause imitates the sound of a pipe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syntactic length, clauses, and linkage to create audible patterns that complement content (e.g., flowing clauses for music, short clauses for abruptness). Re-ordering can destroy the intended musical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of affectation (mannered/affected style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected style is dangerous and falls under three heads: affectation in thought, in words (diction), and in clause structure (e.g., strained metaphors, over-ornamented compounds, forced anapaestic rhythms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for unnatural conceits, strained metaphors, awkward compounds, and affected rhythms; examples: fanciful metaphors that are out of place ('Centaur riding himself') or awkward compounds ('dulcet-coloured rose'). Aim for naturalness and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain style: homely subject-matter, current diction, lucidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain style should be homely and appropriate: diction should be current and familiar; avoid compound/newly-coined words; above all, the style should be lucid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For plain prose use familiar vocabulary, bound (connected) words, simple structure, and clear syntax. Lucidity requires current words and connectedness; avoid loose, disjointed, or obscure structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disjointed/unconnected (histrionic) structure when clarity is required
rubrics_metrics.description: A style wholly disjointed and unconnected is lacking in clearness—broken (histrionic) structures suit acting/debate; compact, consolidated styles are best for reading and literary effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose structure to suit medium: broken, dramatic structure for delivery/acting; compact, conjunction-supported sentences for literary reading. If aiming at 'the reader's favourite' keep structure consolidated and readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialectal/idiomatic form appropriately (Attic terseness vs Doric breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attic dialect is terse and popular, lending itself to witticisms; Doric broadens words and is less suited to comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match dialectal flavor to genre: prefer terse Attic forms for pungent comedy and popular effect; be cautious using dialectal breadth where terseness is needed. Consider historical/diachronic connotations of forms.
